title: Refugee Law, Asylum, and the Principle of Non-Refoulement
seo_title: Refugee Law, Asylum, and Non-Refoulement in International Law
excerpt_139_words: Refugee law, asylum, and non-refoulement protect people who cannot safely rely on their own state. This article explains the 1951 Refugee Convention, 1967 Protocol, refugee definition, persecution, protected grounds, refugee status determination, exclusion, cessation, complementary protection, diplomatic assurances, asylum procedure, border control, detention, family unity, children, gender-sensitive claims, temporary protection, responsibility sharing, and durable solutions. It examines Article 33 non-refoulement, human-rights non-refoulement under the Convention Against Torture, extraterritorial border practices, externalization, safe third country rules, maritime interception, climate-related displacement, and contemporary enforcement gaps. By connecting doctrine, institutions, case studies, and lawyer-facing workflows, it shows how refugee law restrains sovereign border power when return would expose a person to persecution, torture, inhuman treatment, threats to life, or other serious harm.
